where: Section 1, Section 2, Section 3, worked example, quiz Q4 and Q7
problem: Exponents are written inline with no superscript markup, so expressions such as '1000 e−1000tu(t)' and 'e−t/τ' can be read as 'e minus 1000t' or 'e minus t over tau' rather than e raised to a power. The same happens with '1×103 Ω' and '10−6 F' in the worked example.
fix: Use the sup tag for every exponent: h(t)=(1/τ)e<sup>−t/τ</sup>u(t); 1000e<sup>−1000t</sup>u(t) s<sup>−1</sup>; (1×10<sup>3</sup> Ω)(1×10<sup>−6</sup> F); 2×10<sup>−3</sup> s.

problem: The trap mixes two different derivatives. The derivative of e<sup>−t/τ</sup> alone is −(1/τ)e<sup>−t/τ</sup> (negative), while the derivative of s(t)=1−e<sup>−t/τ</sup> is +(1/τ)e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. As written, a student cannot tell whether the mistake is the missing 1/τ factor or the sign.
fix: Rewrite as: Dropping the 1/τ factor or keeping the minus sign. Since s(t)=1−e<sup>−t/τ</sup>, ds/dt = +(1/τ)e<sup>−t/τ</sup>: the derivative of the whole expression is positive even though the derivative of e<sup>−t/τ</sup> alone is negative.

where: Section 2, sentence after the first formula
problem: 'The lower limit −∞ keeps any response before t=0' is unclear. The real purpose of −∞ is to include h(λ) for λ<0, which matters only for noncausal systems; for a causal system those terms are zero anyway.
fix: Say: the lower limit −∞ includes any part of h(λ) at negative times, which matters only for noncausal systems. For a causal system h(λ)=0 there, so the integral runs from 0 to t.
